WRC series.

at the rear, ensuring excellent traction.

Monte Carlo.

defeating entries form Porsche and Lancia.

The car now occupies a page in the history books as the car
that won the first WRC race and series.

Trust me, you’re not likely to forget a car like this.

This is the Chaparral 2J, which was built for
the 1970 Can-Am Series.

What makes it original is found at the rear of the car.

There, you'll find two fans powered by a 274cc engine.

These fans suck the car to the ground
to generate downforce.

They expel the air between the underbody and the road,
creating a suction effect.

For this reason, the 2J i sometimes referred to as
the "fan car.".

Thanks to this ingenious piece of engineering, the car can
take corners at speeds that defy all logic.

The Chaparral 2J set incredible lap times
in all four of the races it entered.

In fact, it even took pole position.

Its Achilles Heel was reliability.

But before it could run a full race, the FIA
changed the rules on aerodynamics...

...deeming the fan system illegal.

One can only imagine what this car could have achieved,
had it been given time to develop.

In 1955, Mercedes-Benz pulled out
of all motorsports events.

It wasn’t until 1988 that it officially
made its return.

the "Silver Arrow."

0x00009B94:
It all goes back some 90 years,
to the Eifel race of 1934.

Back then, the all-white Mercedes F1 was deemed
1kg too heavy for competition.

To reduce its weight, a mechanic scraped off the car's
paint, exposing its aluminum body.

It was this silver-colored car
that ended up winning the race.

This car was dubbed the "Silver Arrow," instantly becoming
a symbol for racing excellence.

Sinc then, silver has been Germany’s national
racing color.

Of course, sponsorship liveries are much
more common today.

And race cars painted in their national colors
are very much a thing of the past.

But if you’re interested in racing history, you should
look into the national race colors of other countries.

the Z, and serve as a symbol of the revival of Nissan itself.

Therefore, it was a car that had to succeed.

Because the Z has been a defining symbol for Nissan through the
years, it naturally embraced the design heritage of the company.

That said, we couldn't give it a retro look.

We needed to retain the essence and spirit
of notabe Nissans of the past...

...while giving it a thoroughly modern character.

The inspiration for the car's design language was
the S30 and the CSP first-generation Silvia.

And, it may be difficult to notice, but there are hints
of the SP Fairlady in the body section.

All of this made the Z33 more modern
and possess different proportions than the S30...

...but I feel it's still instantly
recognizable as a Z from any angle.

from an extremely balanced and pure design.

philosophy applied tothe cars of the Cavallino.

246, such as the progressive wave on the two-wheel arches...

...and the iconic side air intake,
but also the dynamic rear pillars.

four round taillights.

and modern shaping for the time.

The number of cars participating in the 1991 Le Mans race
was only 38, but among those was the new Peugeot 905.

There were also perennial powerhouses like Mercedes-Benz,
Jaguar and Porsche sharing that starting grid.

To take them all on, Mazda entered two 787B race cars.

position, gradually worked its way up the running order...

...until it found its way to the front and finished on top!
It was a dramatic first victory for Japanese manufacturers.

To this day, I haven't forgotten the green and red
Renown livery of that race machine.

This is the car that kick-started Honda’s near 60 years
of Formula 1 Grand Prix history.

After a rough start in 1964, Honda was back in 1965,
with this RA272.

It took the checkered flag at the Mexican Grand Prix
in the final round of the season.

That year happened to be the last one in which F1 machines
were powered by 1.5-liter naturally-aspirated engines.

And let me tell you, the engine that powered this RA272
wa something special!

It was a V-12 with 1495cc of displacement and capable of
a whopping 230 horsepower!

Surprisingly, the displacement per cylinder was a mere
125cc, something that reflected Honda's motorcycle engines.

What’s more, weighing in at 215kg, this super compact
engine was mounted horizontally amidships!

Have you ever heard of such a thing being done
on a Formula 1 car?

But if you give it some thouht, you’ll see that
it actually made a lot of sense.

By mounting an engine on its side, you can shorten
the wheelbase and put less stress on the gearbox.

Compact and easy to handle, Honda’s early attempt
at an F1 machine was an amazing display of engineering.

The track on which the Mexico Grand Prix takes place
is 2300m above sea level.

The low air pressure typically gives engines some
trouble generating power.

In designing the RA272’s powerplant,former aircraft engineer
and Honda’s F1 team leader Yoshio Nakamura...

...made sure it would function at high altitudes,
giving the RA272 an edge over its rivals.

The driver of the winning car was Richie Ginther,
one of the most skilled drivers of his day.

All these ingredients came together in Honda’s first F1 win.
And with that, a glorious history was in the making!

In 1983, after a 15-year break, Honda returned to Formula 1 racing.

For the next 10 years, until it retired again in 1992,
it dominated the competition like no other.

In 1984, a year after its comeback, a Honda-Williams machine
claimed a victory at the American Grand Prix.

The driver of that car was none other than Keke Rosberg,
winner of the 1982 F1 Drivers’ Championship.

Man, did he look super cool when it came time for him
to ascend the podiu.

In any event, the successor of Honda-Williams’ impressive machine
was this McLaren MP4/4.

McLaren began powering its machines with Honda engines
in 1988.

And with drivers Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost, it claimed
the championship that year.

The man responsible for designing the MP4/4 was genius
race-car designer Gordon Murray.

In addition to having a low center of gravity, the McLaren
MP4/4 was equipped with Honda's 1.5-lier RA168E engine.

This turbocharged engine normally produced at 685 horsepower,
but it could be boosted to a maximum 1500 horsepower!

Apparently, the car had trouble with fuel economy,
but Honda’s brilliant engineers found a way to deal with that.

Indeed, they managed to produce the best F1 engine
of the day.

McLaren’s F1 results for the 1988 season were nothing short
of astounding.

To start, they won 15 of 16 races that year!

They alo claimed 15 pole positions, ten 1-2 finishes,
and ten fastest laps.

And with 199 Constructors’ points, they finished
139 points ahead of the second-place team.

When it came to Drivers’ points, Prost had 87 and Senna
had 90, handing him his first Drivers’ title.

This historic win for Senna took place at the Suzuka Circuit
in the Japanese Grand Prix.

It was such a glorious win Soichiro Honda supposedly
said, “If only every day could be this greatv”

Ah, the 1973 Porsche 911 Carrera RS...
What a legend! What a treasure!

This precious gem was designed to compete
in touring car races.

Touring car races are specifically for modified
production cars.

The extent to which a car can be modified
is heavily restricted by FIA guidelines.

But transforming high-performance road cars into
pure race cars...

...is serious business for many automakers, and it has
led to the somereally special machines.

These cars are known as homologation models, which
means they meet FIA requirements for competition.

When the FIA revised its world championship regulations
in 1973...

...Porsche was approved to compete in Group 4 (Gr.4)
of the Grand Touring competition.

The 911 Carrera RS was the homologation model designed
to conquer this Gr.4 class.

The road-going car was made lighter and more powerful
than the standard 911...

...and served as the base for the competition-tuned
911 Carrera RSR!

When the 911 Carrera RSR made its debut in March 1973
at the 12 Hours of Sebring in Florida...

...it turned heads with a dazzling 1-2 finish!

After that, it continued to perform well at

The RX-VISION is a car in which I placed
my car designer life on the line.

I worked on it from the standpoint of really making
the dream sports car I have in my mind.

And one of the most important things for a sports car
is its fundamental structure.

Historic cars that are still popular and beautiful to look at
today all have exceptionally great proportions.

So the first thing we worked on for the RX-VISION
was also the sructure.

and the ability to place proper load on the rear wheels.

That slight unbalance is the hook. It's the secret
to making someone go "Hmm".

The other secret is the reflection of light.

If you look at the RX-VISION as you circle it, I think you'll
notice that the light's reflection moves around like a creature.

Cars are like family or friends to those who are into them.

And it's a very rare industrial product
that runs around on its own.

That makes cars have the same type of existence as animals running
around in the wild, or an athlete running on a field.

And when you think of it that way, I also want cars to be
something that looks beautiful and truly alive in nature.

And for that you need a "sense of life."

So when thinking about what is the sense of life,
that will put cars at one with nature,

we tried to express life in the car with the light's reflections

And those are the type of shapes
that are instilled in the RX-VISION.

In a way this Atenza is my debut work. There were a lot of
obstacles, and it brings back a lot of memories.

I was appointed the general manager of the design division
in 2009, to be the leader of Mazda design,

but I was told about my new position just 2 weeks before, so
I became general manager without any time to be ready.

And the first production car that I worked on,
was this Atenza.

Giventhis major role and responsibility,
this was a state of emergency for me,

but it was just as much a chance as it was a crisis.

It was a time in which the design theme for the next generation of
Mazda's were being considered from almost scratch,

and I thought to make design the major
pillar of Mazda from here and now.

And actually, the development of this car had already progressed
quite a bit under the previous design manager already,

but after thnking that we need to create the philosophy of Mazda
for the next age, and make design itself one of the pillars,

I made the decision to completely change the design
that was already in motion.

To do this it was necessary to redesign things that normally
should not be touched in terms of the development schedules.

As a result, the final design schedule for the production car
was delayed about 10 months...

And I was really scolded badly by the managing drector
of development at the time. A LOT.

At the time I was working on the "SHINARI" concept car
that would be the vision model for the next era,

and I translated the design theme of SHINARI to the production car
because it was a car made alongside the SHINARI.

It's a car that I personally care for a lot, I was
even still driving it until very recently.

Its been over 10 years now, but I think
its a design that doesn't feel old.

The more you work onwstandard cars, the more you understand
the power of design.

And saloons are difficult to design, because
they are the base for all cars.

I think timeless cars of an orthodox category is where
the ability of designers are truly tested.

1JZ-GTE inline-6.

of a luxury sedan with high performance.
